after.problem: The closed curve $C$ is defined as ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=3.$ Find the outward-pointing unit normal vector on $C.$
after.worked_solution:
We can parameterize $C$ as follows:

$$
r(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}],\,t\in [0,2\pi )
$$

To calculate the outward-pointing normal vector of a closed, positively oriented curve, we follow three steps:

**Step 1**: We compute the tangent vector ${r}^{′}(t).$

Differentiating the expression for $r(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Since $C$ is oriented counterclockwise, we rotate ${r}^{′}(t)$ by ${90}^{∘}$ *clockwise* to obtain an outward-pointing normal vector.

The rotation matrix that corresponds to a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation is

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Rotating the vector ${r}^{′}(t)$ by ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise, we get

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 3**: Finally, we normalize the vector found in step 2.

Note that the magnitude of the vector found in step 2 equals the magnitude of ${r}^{′}(t)$ (since they differ only by a rotation).

Now, since 

$$
||{r}^{′}(t)||=\sqrt{(-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}}=\sqrt{3},
$$

and since for our curve $x(t)=\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ and $y(t)=\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,$ it follows that

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{1}{||{r}^{′}(t)||}[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The closed curve C is defined as x2+y2=3. Find the outward-pointing unit normal vector on C.

a
[3x3y]
b
[xy]

EXPLANATION

We can parameterize C as follows:

r(t)=[x(t)y(t)]=[3cos⁡t3sin⁡t],t∈[0,2π)

To calculate the outward-pointing normal vector of a closed, positively oriented curve, we follow three steps:

Step 1: We compute the tangent vector r′(t).

Differentiating the expression for r(t), we get

r′(t)=[x′(t)y′(t)]=[−3sin⁡t3cos⁡t].

Step 2: Since C is oriented counterclockwise, we rotate r′(t) by 90∘ clockwise to obtain an outward-pointing normal vector.

The rotation matrix that corresponds to a 90∘ clockwise rotation is

[01−10].

Rotating the vector r′(t) by 90∘ clockwise, we get

[01−10][−3sin⁡t3cos⁡t]=[3cos⁡t3sin⁡t].

Step 3: Finally, we normalize the vector found in step 2.

Note that the magnitude of the vector found in step 2 equals the magnitude of r′(t) (since they differ only by a rotation).

Now, since

||r′(t)||=(−3sin⁡t)2+(3cos⁡t)2=3,

and since for our curve x(t)=3cos⁡t and y(t)=3sin⁡t, it follows that

n=1||r′(t)||[3cos⁡t3sin⁡t]=13[3cos⁡t3sin⁡t]=13[xy].

content.knowledge_point: Calculating an Outward-Pointing Unit Normal Vector for a Positively Oriented Curve
content.problem: The closed curve $C$ is defined as ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=3.$ Find the outward-pointing unit normal vector on $C.$
content.worked_solution:
We can parameterize $C$ as follows:

$$
r(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}],\,t\in [0,2\pi )
$$

To calculate the outward-pointing normal vector of a closed, positively oriented curve, we follow three steps:

**Step 1**: We compute the tangent vector ${r}^{′}(t).$

Differentiating the expression for $r(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Since $C$ is oriented counterclockwise, we rotate ${r}^{′}(t)$ by ${90}^{∘}$ *clockwise* to obtain an outward-pointing normal vector.

The rotation matrix that corresponds to a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation is

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Rotating the vector ${r}^{′}(t)$ by ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise, we get

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 3**: Finally, we normalize the vector found in step 2.

Note that the magnitude of the vector found in step 2 equals the magnitude of ${r}^{′}(t)$ (since they differ only by a rotation).

Now, since 

$$
||{r}^{′}(t)||=\sqrt{(-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}}=\sqrt{3},
$$

and since for our curve $x(t)=\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ and $y(t)=\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,$ it follows that

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{1}{||{r}^{′}(t)||}[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ \sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

content.worked_solution:
For convenience, we express $r(t)$ in column vector notation:

$$
r(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}15\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 7\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]
$$

To calculate the outward-pointing normal vector of a closed, *negatively* oriented curve, we follow three steps:

**Step 1**: We compute the tangent vector ${r}^{′}(t).$

Differentiating the expression for $r(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}15\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ -7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Since $C$ is oriented clockwise, we rotate ${r}^{′}(t)$ by ${90}^{∘}$ *counterclockwise* to obtain an outward-pointing normal vector.

The rotation matrix that corresponds to a ${90}^{∘}$ counterclockwise rotation is

$$
R=[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Rotating the vector ${r}^{′}(t)$ by ${90}^{∘}$ counterclockwise, we get

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}15\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ -7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}7\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 15\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 3**: Finally, we normalize the vector found in step 2.

Note that the magnitude of the vector found in step 2 equals the magnitude of ${r}^{′}(t)$ (since they differ only by a rotation). Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{1}{||{r}^{′}(t)||}[\begin{aligned}7\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 15\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]=\frac{7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+15\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j}{||{r}^{′}(t)||}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that $b(t)=15\operatorname{cos}⁡t.$

content.problem:
The closed curve $C$ is defined as $r(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ).$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector for $C$ can be expressed as

$$
n=\frac{a(t)\,i+b(t)\,j}{||{r}^{′}(t)||}.
$$

Find the function $b(t).$

*Hint: Observe that $C$ is traversed clockwise.*
content.worked_solution:
For convenience, we express $r(t)$ in column vector notation:

$$
r(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]
$$

To calculate the outward-pointing normal vector of a closed, *negatively* oriented curve, we follow three steps:

**Step 1**: We compute the tangent vector ${r}^{′}(t).$

Differentiating the expression for $r(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ -2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Since $C$ is oriented clockwise, we rotate ${r}^{′}(t)$ by ${90}^{∘}$ *counterclockwise* to obtain an outward-pointing normal vector.

The rotation matrix that corresponds to a ${90}^{∘}$ counterclockwise rotation is

$$
R=[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Rotating the vector ${r}^{′}(t)$ by ${90}^{∘}$ counterclockwise, we get

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ -2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 3**: Finally, we normalize the vector found in step 2.

Note that the magnitude of the vector found in step 2 equals the magnitude of ${r}^{′}(t)$ (since they differ only by a rotation). Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{1}{||{r}^{′}(t)||}[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]=\frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j}{||{r}^{′}(t)||}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that $b(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t.$

after.problem: The closed curve $C$ is defined as ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=36.$ Find the outward-pointing unit normal vector on $C.$
after.worked_solution:
We can parameterize $C$ as follows:

$$
r(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}6\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 6\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}],\,t\in [0,2\pi )
$$

To calculate the outward-pointing normal vector of a closed, positively oriented curve, we follow three steps:

**Step 1**: We compute the tangent vector ${r}^{′}(t).$

Differentiating the expression for $r(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-6\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 6\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Since $C$ is oriented counterclockwise, we rotate ${r}^{′}(t)$ by ${90}^{∘}$ *clockwise* to obtain an outward-pointing normal vector.

The rotation matrix that corresponds to a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation is

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Rotating the vector ${r}^{′}(t)$ by ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise, we get

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-6\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 6\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}6\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 6\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 3**: Finally, we normalize the vector found in step 2.

Note that the magnitude of the vector found in step 2 equals the magnitude of ${r}^{′}(t)$ (since they differ only by a rotation).

Now, since 

$$
||{r}^{′}(t)||=\sqrt{(-6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(6\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}}=6,
$$

and since for our curve $x(t)=6\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ and $y(t)=6\operatorname{sin}⁡t,$ it follows that

$$

content.problem: The closed curve $C$ is defined as ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=36.$ Find the outward-pointing unit normal vector on $C.$
content.worked_solution:
We can parameterize $C$ as follows:

$$
r(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}6\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 6\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}],\,t\in [0,2\pi )
$$

To calculate the outward-pointing normal vector of a closed, positively oriented curve, we follow three steps:

**Step 1**: We compute the tangent vector ${r}^{′}(t).$

Differentiating the expression for $r(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-6\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 6\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Since $C$ is oriented counterclockwise, we rotate ${r}^{′}(t)$ by ${90}^{∘}$ *clockwise* to obtain an outward-pointing normal vector.

The rotation matrix that corresponds to a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation is

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Rotating the vector ${r}^{′}(t)$ by ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise, we get

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-6\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 6\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}6\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 6\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 3**: Finally, we normalize the vector found in step 2.

Note that the magnitude of the vector found in step 2 equals the magnitude of ${r}^{′}(t)$ (since they differ only by a rotation).

Now, since 

$$
||{r}^{′}(t)||=\sqrt{(-6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(6\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}}=6,
$$

and since for our curve $x(t)=6\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ and $y(t)=6\operatorname{sin}⁡t,$ it follows that

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{1}{||{r}^{′}(t)||}[\begin{aligned}6\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 6\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{6}[\begin{aligned}6\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 6\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{6}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$
